newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Cyprus talks resume amid gloom over outcome.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus talks resume amid gloom over outcome.

text.p: Leaders of the two main communities involved in the 34-year-old Cyprus problem began a week of talks on Monday but diplomats said prospects for movement towards a solution looked dim.

Gloom was deepened by Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash who, after arriving in Switzerland on Sunday, insisted on absolute political equality with 78-year-old Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides -- anathema to the Greek Cypriots.

"There really seems little chance of any sort of breakthrough," said one envoy close to the talks, being held in a luxury hotel in extensive grounds amid high security in the village of Glion overlooking Montreux and Lake Geneva.

The discussions, due to last five days and subject to a media blackout, are being held under United Nations mediation and follow a first round last month at Troutbeck, near New York, which appeared to make no headway.

The 73-year-old Denktash, head of the breakaway northern Turkish Cypriot administration recognised only by Turkey, told Reuters in an interview on Sunday the talks could proceed only on the basis of political equality on paper and in effect.

He called on U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan's special adviser for Cyprus, former Ecuadorean Foreign Minister Diego Cordovez who will be supervising the talks, to agree to a new track in the negotiations on the basis of equality.
"We have come with goodwill to defend what is ours," Denktash said during a stopover in Geneva.

"The attempt to set up a federal partnership failed so far because a federal partnership can only be established between two equals. That equality has been destroyed by the world by treating the Greek Cypriot partner as the government of all."

Denktash added: "That has to be corrected if a solution is expected. It's no use dwelling on the same procedure. A new track has to be found on basis of absolute political equality -- political equality not only on paper merely but in effect."
That means rotating presidency, real power-sharing with the Greek Cypriots in government and sovereign equality, he said.
Such ideas are vehemently opposed by the Greek Cypriots on the grounds that the Turkish Cypriots account for only 18 percent of the population.

Public positions have become more entrenched since Troutbeck. Stakes are also higher as Cyprus prepares for entry talks with the European Union next year and Turkey says it will move towards partial integration with the north.
But Clerides himself made no press statement on arrival in Switzerland, heading straight for Glion.

Denktash accused the EU of getting in the way of a deal and threatened to pull out of the negotiations: "If the EU talks start, the intercommunal talks will stop and that will be the end of the matter," he said.
Greek and Turkish Cypriots have been estranged since 1963, three years after independence from Britain, when a government representing both communities broke apart amid violence.
They have been separated since 1974 when Turkey invaded the northern third of the island in response to a coup in the capital Nicosia, backed by the junta then ruling Greece.
The international community's trump card in the talks is U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke, waiting on the sidelines to step in at the right time with his tough, result-oriented diplomacy.
If the latest round of talks fail, diplomats fear the east Mediterranean island could end up being more divided than ever.
